subject: math
cluster: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models
intro: These problems involve dependent (without-replacement) draws, compound conditions, and simulations. For without-replacement draws, remember that the total number of items shrinks after the first pick, so the second-stage probability changes. For simulations, define a trial carefully and estimate the probability as the fraction of trials in which the event occurs.

items.prompt: A bag holds $4$ red and $3$ blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. Find $P(\text{both red})$, written as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: First draw: $7$ marbles, $4$ red, so $P(\text{1st red})=\frac{4}{7}$.
After removing one red, $6$ marbles remain with $3$ red, so $P(\text{2nd red})=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$.

items.prompt: A drawer contains $5$ black socks and $3$ white socks. Two socks are pulled out without replacement. Find $P(\text{both white})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: First draw: $8$ socks, $3$ white, so $P(\text{1st white})=\frac{3}{8}$.
After removing one white, $7$ socks remain with $2$ white, so $P(\text{2nd white})=\frac{2}{7}$.

items.prompt: A box has $6$ green and $4$ yellow markers. Two markers are taken without replacement. Find $P(\text{first green and second yellow})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: First draw green: $10$ markers, $6$ green, so $P=\frac{6}{10}=\frac{3}{5}$.
After removing one green, $9$ markers remain with $4$ yellow, so $P(\text{2nd yellow})=\frac{4}{9}$.

items.prompt: A bag has $3$ red and $2$ blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. Find $P(\text{one red and one blue, in either order})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: These two outcomes are different, so add them: $\frac{3}{10}+\frac{3}{10}=\frac{6}{10}$.

items.prompt: A deck of $12$ cards has $4$ aces. Two cards are dealt without replacement. Find $P(\text{no aces})$ (neither card is an ace) as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: After removing one non-ace, $11$ cards remain with $7$ non-aces, so $P=\frac{7}{11}$.
Multiply: $\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{7}{11}=\frac{14}{33}$, which is already in lowest terms.

items.prompt: Using the bag from problem $5$ ($4$ aces, $8$ non-aces, two cards dealt without replacement), find $P(\text{at least one ace})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: Use the complement: $P(\text{at least one ace})=1-P(\text{no aces})$.
This fraction is already in lowest terms.

items.prompt: A committee of $2$ students is chosen at random from a group of $4$ girls and $2$ boys (without replacement). Find $P(\text{the committee is both boys})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: There are $6$ students total, $2$ of them boys.
After one boy is chosen, $5$ students remain with $1$ boy, so $P=\frac{1}{5}$.

items.prompt: A jar contains $5$ red, $3$ green, and $2$ blue candies. Two candies are eaten without replacement. Find $P(\text{both the same color})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.
Three marbles are drawn without replacement from a bag of $4$ red and $2$ white marbles. Find $P(\text{all three red})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: First red: $\frac{4}{6}$. Second red: $\frac{3}{5}$. Third red: $\frac{2}{4}$.

items.prompt: A spelling bee has $7$ finalists: $3$ from Lincoln School and $4$ from Park School. Two finalists are chosen at random (without replacement) to go first and second. Find $P(\text{both chosen are from Park School})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: After one Park student is chosen, $6$ remain with $3$ from Park, so $P=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$.

items.prompt: A basketball player makes a free throw $70\%$ of the time. To estimate the probability that she makes both of her next two free throws, a student assigns the digits $0$-$6$ to a make and $7$-$9$ to a miss, then reads pairs of digits as one trial (each digit is one shot). Here are $10$ trials: $43,\ 81,\ 25,\ 60,\ 97,\ 12,\ 58,\ 34,\ 76,\ 09$. Estimate $P(\text{both made})$ from this simulation, as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: A 'make' is a digit $0$-$6$; a 'miss' is $7$-$9$. Both made means both digits in the pair are $0$-$6$.
Check each trial: $43$ both made; $81$ has $8$ (miss); $25$ both made; $60$ both made; $97$ both miss; $12$ both made; $58$ has $8$ (miss); $34$ both made; $76$ has $7$ (miss); $09$ has $9$ (miss).
Trials with both made: $43, 25, 60, 12, 34$, which is $5$ of the $10$ trials.

items.prompt: A cereal company puts one of $3$ equally likely prizes (A, B, C) in each box. To estimate the probability of getting all $3$ different prizes in $3$ boxes, a student assigns $1\to A$, $2\to B$, $3\to C$ and ignores the digits $0$ and $4$-$9$. Reading the random digits and grouping the kept digits into sets of three, the first $8$ valid trials are: $123,\ 112,\ 231,\ 333,\ 132,\ 122,\ 211,\ 223$. Estimate $P(\text{all three different prizes})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: All three different means the trial contains one each of $1, 2, 3$ in some order.
Check each trial: $123$ all different; $112$ repeats $1$; $231$ all different; $333$ all same; $132$ all different; $122$ repeats $2$; $211$ repeats $1$; $223$ repeats $2$.
Trials with all three different: $123, 231, 132$, which is $3$ of the $8$ trials.
Estimate: $\frac{3}{8}$, which is already in lowest terms.

items.prompt: Using the same setup as problem $9$ ($4$ red and $2$ white marbles, three drawn without replacement), find $P(\text{exactly two of the three are red})$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: 'Exactly two red' means two red and one white among the three draws. The white can come 1st, 2nd, or 3rd.

items.prompt: A class has $10$ students: $6$ who walk to school and $4$ who ride the bus. The teacher picks $2$ students at random (without replacement) to lead an activity. The theoretical probability that both walk is $\frac{1}{3}$. In a simulation, the experiment was repeated $50$ times and 'both walk' happened in $18$ of those trials. (a) Write the experimental probability as a fraction in lowest terms. (b) Is the experimental probability greater than or less than the theoretical probability?

steps: (b) Compare to theoretical $\frac{1}{3}$. Write both with denominator $75$: $\frac{9}{25}=\frac{27}{75}$ and $\frac{1}{3}=\frac{25}{75}$.
Since $\frac{27}{75}>\frac{25}{75}$, the experimental probability is greater than the theoretical probability.

items.prompt: A bag contains $3$ red, $4$ blue, and $5$ green chips. Three chips are drawn without replacement. Find $P(\text{one of each color})$ (one red, one blue, and one green, in any order) as a fraction in lowest terms.

steps: There are $12$ chips total. One specific order, say red then blue then green, has probability $\frac{3}{12}\cdot\frac{4}{11}\cdot\frac{5}{10}=\frac{60}{1320}$.
Every order of the three colors (R,B,G), (R,G,B), (B,R,G), (B,G,R), (G,R,B), (G,B,R) gives the same product $\frac{60}{1320}$.
There are $6$ such orders, so multiply: $6\cdot\frac{60}{1320}=\frac{360}{1320}$.
